newsitem.title: USA: Southern buys stake in Asian utility for $2.7 billion.
newsitem.headline: Southern buys stake in Asian utility for $2.7 billion.

text.p: Southern Co. said Wednesday its Southern Electric International unit has agreed to buy a majority interest in Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd. (CEPA) in a deal worth $2.7 billion.
Consolidated Electric, one of Asia's largest independent power producers, is 60.4 percent owned by Hong Kong-based Hopewell Holdings Ltd.

"Under the agreement, CEPA shareholders will receive $2.1 billion from Southern and $600 million in dividends for 80 percent of the company. Hopewell will become the largest minority shareholder of CEPA," Southern said.
Company officials were not immediately available to explain details of the planned transaction.
Atlanta-based Southern's move is the latest move by U.S. power companies, such as Houston-based Enron Corp., to get into power projects overseas.

"Combining the assets of Southern Electric International and CEPA will create one of the world's largest independent power producers, supplying electricity to the heart of Asia -- including three of the world's most populated countries -- as well as Europe, North America and South America," said Southern Chief Executive Officer A.W. Dahlberg.
Consolidated Electric Asia owns and operates electric power generating plants in China and the Philippines with projects under development in Pakistan and Indonesia.
The company was established in 1993 as a holding company for Hopewell's electric power projects.

Southern, the largest producer of electricity in the United States, is the parent of five Southeast electric utilities: Alabama Power, Georgia Power, Gulf Power, Mississippi Power and Savannah Electric.

CEPA's Asian power projects "bring a greater regional diversity and geographical balance" to Southern's international holdings, Dahlberg said. Southern operates electric power facilities in England, Argentina, Chile, the Bahamas, Trinidad and Tobago.

"Two years ago, we established a goal for Southern Electric International to become one of the world's top independent energy companies as a means of enhancing Southern Company's long-term growth and income potential and shareholder value," Dahlberg said. "This partnership with CEPA is a significant step toward that goal."
Southern said the transaction was subject to approvals by the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong and CEPA shareholders.
Early this year, Southern sold a minority stake in the British regional electric company, South Western Electricity, to a unit of Pennsylvania Power & Light for $189 million.
Southern, which paid $1.7 billion to acquire the British firm in 1995, had stated that it wanted to sell a stake of up to 49 percent in South Western to fuel its acquisition plans in Europe.
Southern stock fell 50 cents to $22 on the New York Stock Exchange.
